name: AMASS: Archive of Motion Capture as Surface Shapes
description: A large and varied database of human motion that unifies 15 different optical marker-based motion capture datasets within a common framework and parameterization by representing them as SMPL body model parameters with shape, pose, and soft-tissue motion. The dataset contains 42 hours of mocap, 346 subjects, and 11451 motions.
creator: Naureen Mahmood; Nima Ghorbani; Nikolaus F. Troje; Gerard Pons-Moll; Michael J. Black
citeAs: Naureen Mahmood, Nima Ghorbani, Nikolaus F. Troje, Gerard Pons-Moll, Michael J. Black. AMASS: Archive of Motion Capture as Surface Shapes. arXiv:1904.03278v1, 2019.
rai:dataCollection: AMASS was created by combining 15 existing motion capture datasets into one large dataset and mapping archival marker-based optical mocap data into a common SMPL representation using MoSh++. The public datasets were downloaded from the internet; several other datasets were obtained privately or recorded by the authors themselves. Due to inherent problems with mocap, such as swapped and mislabeled markers, the authors manually inspected the results and either corrected or held out problems. The paper also introduces a new dataset, Synchronized Scans and Markers (SSM), collected with an OptiTrack mocap system synchronized with a 4D scanning system to tune and evaluate MoSh++.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Physical data collection, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During a mocap session, markers may get occluded by the body due to pose. If multiple markers of a particular body part are occluded simultaneously, the optimization may result in unreliable and implausible poses. The method introduces a coefficient based on the number of missing markers in a frame to increase the pose prior weight when markers are missing.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data are 15 optical marker-based human motion capture datasets with varying marker sets ranging from 37 to 91 markers. Publicly available datasets were downloaded from the internet, while several others were obtained privately or recorded by the authors. For SSM, raw data consisted of synchronized OptiTrack mocap recordings with 67 reflective markers and high-resolution 4D body scans captured by a 3dMD 4D scanning system.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors used MoSh++ to map marker data from the source datasets into common SMPL pose, shape, and soft-tissue parameters. They unified datasets recorded with different numbers and placements of markers into a single format. They manually inspected outputs and either corrected or held out problems such as swapped and mislabeled markers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To create AMASS, the authors converted sparse marker data into SMPL body model parameters using MoSh++. Each frame includes SMPL 3D shape parameters, DMPL soft-tissue coefficients, and full SMPL pose parameters including hand articulations. For SSM, the mocap system was synchronized and calibrated with a 4D scanning system. Subjects wore minimal clothing to avoid artifacts due to sliding cloth, and markers were placed directly on the skin wherever possible.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset does not use conventional human semantic labels; instead, MoSh++ fits a body model to sparse mocap markers to produce per-frame SMPL shape, pose, and DMPL soft-tissue parameters. When hand markers are present, MoSh++ fits hand pose using SMPL-H. The authors also manually inspected results and corrected or held out sequences with swapped or mislabeled markers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors evaluated and tuned MoSh++ hyperparameters using the SSM dataset with synchronized 3D scans as ground truth. They used cross-validation and scan-to-model distances between 3D scans and reconstructed meshes to select weights and model dimensionality. They also note that adding more shape or dynamic coefficients decreases marker error but overfits to markers, causing higher error relative to ground truth shape.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset will be publicly available to the research community at http://amass.is.tue.mpg.de. The authors state that with MoSh++ it is easy to add more data and they will continue to expand the dataset. They will support the community in adding new captures as long as they can be similarly shared, and state that they will continuously incorporate more mocap data contributed by the authors and the community.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Body shape; hand articulation; soft-tissue motion; motion capture recordings; 4D body scans. The dataset includes over 300 subjects and the paper notes that SSM contains three subjects with varying body shapes.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to enable machine learning applications in animation and computer vision, including generating synthetic training data for computer vision tasks. The authors argue that having a body model makes it possible to texture and render virtual bodies in different scenes, which is useful for many tasks.
rai:dataBiases: The source datasets are often narrowly focused on particular classes of motions. The datasets vary in format, kinematic structure, marker sets, and laboratory-specific procedures. For SSM, the dataset consists of only three subjects with varying body shapes, and two of the three subjects were professional models.
rai:dataLimitations: Existing mocap datasets are small and motions limited; AMASS addresses this but still inherits inherent mocap problems such as swapped, mislabeled, and occluded markers. The source datasets use varying marker sets and laboratory-specific procedures. Current runtime for MoSh++ is not real-time. The paper states there is no ground-truth data for evaluating accuracy of hand articulation. SSM used for evaluation contains only three subjects, and future work will extend it to include articulated hands.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is readily useful for animation, visualization, and generating training data for deep learning. It is intended to enable new applications that require large amounts of training data and can support machine learning for animation and computer vision. Each frame provides SMPL pose, shape, and soft-tissue parameters; users who only care about pose can ignore body shape and soft tissue deformations, and users can normalize all bodies to the same shape if desired.
